title: Caleb Flynn: Former ‘American Idol’ contestant found guilty of murder | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Caleb Flynn, a former worship leader and “American Idol” contestant, was found guilty of murdering his wife, Ashley Flynn, and all other charges Tuesday afterprosecutors argued he fatally shot herand staged the scene to look like an intruder did it.

The jury found Flynn, 40, guilty of all nine charges, including aggravated murder, murder, felony murder, felonious assault and tampering with evidence.

He shook his head, sobbed and wiped his nose as the guilty verdict was read. He was then put in handcuffs and escorted from the courtroom.

Flynn faces a sentence of life in prison without parole, and a sentencing hearing was set for October 5. The jury deliberated for about two hours before reaching the verdict.

The case stems from the early morning hours of February 16, when Flynn called 911 to report his wife Ashley had been fatally shot in their Tipp City, Ohio, home by an unknown intruder.

Prosecutors alleged Flynn murdered his wife and staged the crime scene, pointing to his affair with a fellow worship leader at his church as a motive. During the trial, jurors visited the family’s home, watched police bodycam footage from the night of Ashley’s death and heard Flynn’s messages to his24-year-old mistress.

“I was up until 4 a.m. last night crying, literally thinking of ways to kill her and not go to jail,” Flynn wrote in a message to his paramour in August 2025.

The prosecution said Flynn wanted to frame a “faceless” intruder for his wife’s killing in order to keep his relationship with his mistress, full custody of his two daughters, his “lucrative” job at his wife’s family business and his position as a worship leader.

“The evidence does not lead to some unknown intruder who vanished into the night. It leads straight to the defendant,” Miami County Assistant Prosecuting Attorney Matt Joseph said in closing arguments.

In the defense’s closing, attorney Patrick Mulligan said prosecutors proved Flynn had an affair, but they did not prove he killed his wife, noting themissing murder weapon.

“This simply is proven versus not proven, and respectfully I would suggest this is a matter of not proven, and therefore worthy of a verdict of not guilty,” he said.

Flynn appeared emotional, wiping tears and sniffling as both the prosecution and defense delivered their closing arguments, which followed nearly two weeks of testimony. The prosecution called 40 witnesses over seven days of testimony, while the defense did not call any.

The guilty verdicts represent a steep fall from grace for Flynn, who had a short stint on the show “American Idol” 13 years ago.

“The thing that makes me unique, you know, I absolutely love the Lord. I love my wife more than anything,” he said inan interview for the show. “She’s very, very pretty, just – woof, I love her.”

Ashley’s family said the verdicts brought “justice and accountability for Ashley’s death,” but acknowledged “no verdict can bring Ashley back, give the girls back their Mother, or erase the pain our family has endured.”

The family believes, they said in a statement, that Ashley will not be defined by the way her life ended, describing her as a woman who “loved Jesus with her whole heart” and loved being a mother.

“We refuse to let the evil that ended Ashley’s life have the final word in her story,” the statement said. “Our faith does not erase our grief, but it carries us through it.”

“We know Ashley is home with the Lord she loved and served.”

In a statement, Flynn’s defense attorney expressed “deep respect for the jury system in the United States.”

“At the same time, we are disappointed with the results,” Mulligan said. “Not all juries answer questions correctly. I am confident that this decision by the jury will be tested as many times as is required during the appeal process, which will undoubtedly begin after sentencing.”

The prosecution focused its case on Flynn’s secret affair and disproving his claim that an intruder broke into their home.

The case began in the early morning hours of February 16 when Flynn called 911 and reported, “Somebody broke into my home and shot my wife.”

Police raced to the scene and found Ashley dead in her bedroom of two gunshot wounds. Flynn told investigators he had been lying in his daughters’ bedroom when he heard a gunshot. He said he noticed the garage side door was flung open, and then found his wife dead in the bed.

“I went in their room, and I laid down with them for – I don’t even know how long, and that’s when I heard it,” Flynn told officers in a conversation captured on police bodycam footage.

“When I finally got up, the door leading to the garage was open, but I didn’t see anybody,” he said.

The center console of Flynn’s truck, where he said he stored his handgun, was open when police arrived, according to David Hammond, a special agent with the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation.

Investigators did not find any trace of an intruder fleeing the area, and the damage to the garage side door was inconsistent with a typical break-in, police testified. The firearm has never been found.

In an interview later that day, Flynn told an investigator he and his wife had no marital problems “whatsoever.”

Alleigha Botner, 24, testified across two days about her and Flynn’s nearly two-year romantic relationship. She read aloud their text messages in which Flynn described how much he hated his wife and expressed a desire to rid her from his life.

“I just want her dead and gone,” Flynn wrote to the mistress in early 2025.

In a spree of texts the day before his wife’s death, Flynn assured Botner he was going to get a divorce the following day. When Botner learned of Ashley’s death the next morning, she said her “heart started pounding.”

““It seemed like too much of a coincidence that the day he’s divorcing her, she’s just dead all of a sudden.””

— Alleigha Botner

Hours after Ashley’s death,Flynn and Botner metat his in-laws’ house, where members of their church were gathered. When Botner arrived, Flynn hugged her, she testified.

“It didn’t happen the way we thought it would, did it?” Flynn said, according to her testimony.

Botner asked Flynn a lot of questions about the shooting, she testified, telling the court she was “very suspicious.”

According to Botner’s testimony, Flynn told her he had been sleeping on the couch when he heard a gunshot and ran straight to the garage, where he saw the side door open. He said he then found Ashley dead in the bedroom, Botner testified. That account appeared to contradict Flynn’s statement to law enforcement in which he said he was lying in his daughters’ bedroom when he heard a gunshot.

Other witnesses testified about evidence prosecutors say undermines Flynn’s initial story to police. A digital forensics examiner said Flynn’s electronic devices recorded roughly 200 steps at intermittent times in the hour before he called 911 to report his wife had been shot. Around 2:30 a.m., when Flynn called 911, another 346 steps were recorded.

Ashley’s father, Todd Smith, said Flynn’s story simply didn’t make sense.

“Nothing makes sense to me,” Smith testified. “Why would somebody break in, go in and get into the truck, go walk in there, shoot my daughter, and then run out? If it was a burglary, why weren’t they going around the whole house?”
